relevance_reason: Defines a new ARCND locus (ARCND4) on 7p: a 430-kb tandem duplication involving HDAC9/TWIST1 regulatory elements in a four-generation Brazilian family, with functional iPSC studies.

findings.statement: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) studied a previously reported non-consanguineous four-generation Brazilian family with 11 members showing typical features of auriculocondylar syndrome. Of the 10 documented, most had question mark ears (8 of 10), microstomia (8 of 10), and micrognathia (6 of 10), with considerable intrafamilial variability. The patients did not have large, open fontanelles, the hallmark of trisomy 7p.
quotes: The Brazilian family (referred to as F1; online supplemental table 1) is a non-consanguineous family with 11 members showing the typical characteristics of ARCND.
Of those documented, the majority presented with question mark ears (8 of 10), microstomia (8 of 10) and micrognathia (6 of 10), with considerable intrafamilial variability observed.
We note, however, that our patients did not have large, open fontanelles, the hallmark feature of trisomy 7p

findings.statement: In the Brazilian ARCND family, in which Sanger sequencing of PLCB4, GNAI3, and EDN1 revealed no pathogenic variants, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) performed genomewide SNP linkage analysis (9 affected, 3 unaffected genotyped) under an autosomal dominant model and found a maximum LOD score of 2.88 (maximum theoretical 2.93) in a 17.6-Mb region on chromosome 7 (chr7:14,395,902-32,017,194, hg38), narrowed by microsatellite markers to chr7:14,395,902-28,158,440. Gene prioritization ranked TWIST1 as the top candidate in the region.
quotes: Sanger sequencing of PLCB4, GNAI3 and EDN1 did not reveal any pathogenic variants in the coding regions, 5′ UTRs (untranslated regions) or splice sites of these genes, suggesting that a different locus might underlie the ARCND in the family.

The highest LOD score (2.88), which is close to the threshold value of ≥3.0 for significance and the maximum theoretical LOD score for this family (2.93), was observed in a region of about 17.6 Mb on chromosome 7 (chr7:14395902–32017194 (hg38); table 1).
Genotyping of microsatellite markers narrowed the chromosome 7 linkage region to chr7:14395902–28158440 (hg38) (online supplemental figure 2).

findings.statement: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found no causative variants by whole-exome sequencing in 4 affected family members (a synonymous TRIL variant did not segregate). Targeted resequencing of a 2.4-Mb region around TWIST1 identified a 430,302-bp tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) beginning about 280 kb telomeric to TWIST1 and covering most of HDAC9; breakpoint PCR and Sanger sequencing showed segregation with the phenotype, with all unaffected individuals negative, suggesting full penetrance. Full-length catalytically active HDAC9 isoforms were predicted to be disrupted.
quotes: Targeted resequencing of a 2.4 Mb region around TWIST1 revealed no potential pathogenic variants in TWIST1, but did detect a tandem duplication within HDAC9 that was only present within the three affected family members tested
The duplication spanned 430 302 bp (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) telomeric to TWIST1, covering most of the HDAC9 gene.

Breakpoint amplification and Sanger sequencing within the family demonstrated segregation of the duplication with the phenotype (figure 1B). All unaffected individuals were negative, suggesting full penetrance in this family

findings.statement: Capture-C analysis in human embryonic calvarial mesenchymal cells, using the TWIST1 promoter as viewpoint, by Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) showed multiple cis contacts, with the highest frequency telomeric of TWIST1 within HDAC9 and the duplicated region, implying that the region contains TWIST1 regulatory elements (including enhancer eTw6) and providing a possible pathogenic mechanism.
quotes: The highest frequency of interactions was telomeric of TWIST1, particularly within the HDAC9 gene and the region spanned by the duplication (figure 1A). This implies that this region contains regulatory elements involved in the control of TWIST1 expression, providing a possible pathogenic mechanism for the duplication.

findings.statement: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) noted 19 DECIPHER patients with copy-number gains in the region; 7 had ear malformations and 7 micrognathia, mostly with larger duplications including the TWIST1 enhancer eTW6. One 179-kb duplication (276644) lying entirely within the ARCND duplicated region but not spanning the TWIST1 regulatory elements was not associated with ARCND features.
quotes: Nevertheless, 7 out of 19 have descriptions that include ear malformation among other features
Interestingly, one of the DECIPHER duplications (276644; 179 kb) is enclosed entirely within the ARCND duplicated region; however, this patient does not have ARCND clinical features

findings.statement: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) generated iPSCs from 3 affected family members and controls and differentiated them into neural crest cells (iNCCs) and mesenchymal stem-like cells (nMSCs). Patient iNCCs showed increased HDAC9 (3.15-fold) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold) mRNA and a 4.3-fold decrease in migratory capacity, with no cell-cycle difference. Patient nMSCs showed reduced ALP activity (20.3-fold decrease) and expression and subtly reduced matrix mineralization, indicating delayed or impaired osteogenic differentiation; the authors suggested that TWIST1 deregulation contributes to ARCND via compromised neural crest migration and osteogenesis.
quotes: However, an increase in HDAC9 (3.15-fold, unpaired t-test p=0.009) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold, unpaired t-test p=0.03) mRNA was observed in the ARCND-iNCC (figure 2A, B) compared with controls (unpaired t-test).
a significant decrease in migratory capacity of ARCND iNCCs was observed compared with controls (4.3-fold decrease, Student’s t-test, p=0.0009)

Our data showed that during osteogenic differentiation, ALP enzymatic activity was significantly diminished in ARCND-nMSCs after 9 days of osteoinduction (decrease of 20.3-fold, paired t-test p=0.029; figure 3A, B).

relevance_reason: Abstract describes a large ACS family (F1) and linkage of ACS to 1p21.1-q23.3 in a second family (F2), with F1 unlinked. This gives evidence for genetic heterogeneity of auriculocondylar syndrome, which is relevant context for a further ARCND locus.

findings.statement: Masotti et al. (2008) described a multigeneration family (F1) with 11 individuals affected by auriculocondylar syndrome and confirmed variable features within the family. Facial asymmetry was highly prevalent among the patients. The authors noted that this feature had not been highlighted in earlier ACS reports. ACS is characterized by malformed 'question mark' ears, prominent cheeks, microstomia, an abnormal temporomandibular joint and mandibular condyle hypoplasia.
quotes: We herein describe a new multigeneration family with 11 affected individuals (F1), in whom we confirm intra-familial clinical variability.
Facial asymmetry, a clinical feature not highlighted in other ACS reports, was highly prevalent among the patients reported here.
is characterized by malformed ears ('question mark ears'), prominent cheeks, microstomia, abnormal temporomandibular joint, and mandibular condyle hypoplasia

findings.statement: Masotti et al. (2008) performed linkage analysis in two large ACS families, F1 and F2. Segregation analysis excluded the Treacher Collins syndrome, oculoauriculovertebral spectrum and Townes-Brocks syndrome loci. A genomewide search then found evidence of linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3 in family F2 (maximum lod score 3.01 at theta = 0), which defined the first ACS locus (ACS1).
quotes: Through segregation analysis, we first excluded three known loci associated with disorders of first and second pharyngeal arches (Treacher Collins syndrome, oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, and Townes-Brocks syndrome).
we performed a wide genome search and we observed evidence of linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3 in F2 (LOD max 3.01 at theta=0).

findings.statement: Masotti et al. (2008) found that the 1p21.1-q23.3 locus linked in family F2 was not linked to the phenotype segregating in family F1. They concluded that ACS is genetically heterogeneous, with at least two loci responsible for the phenotype.
quotes: Interestingly, this locus was not linked to the phenotype segregating in F1.
showed evidence for genetic heterogeneity, suggesting that there are at least two loci responsible for this phenotype.
